fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. Isaiah says, "From the ends of the earth we hear singing: “Glory to the Righteous One.”" (Isaiah 24:16) After all that ruin, a song rises from the farthest places. Now THAT is a sound worth hearing.

That's a real treaty from another part of the Bible, friend (Joshua 9:15), but it isn't in this verse. Isaiah names "the laws," "the decrees" and "…the everlasting covenant." The Gibeon treaty isn't on his list. You went looking in a different chapter's pantry.
I love the energy, friend, but that's not what the verse says. Isaiah says the merrymakers "now groan," and the very next verse says the tambourines have ceased. The harp is silent too.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "strong drink is bitter to those who consume it." (Isaiah 24:9) That's the word that fits the blank. The verse also says the people no longer sing and drink wine.
Sweet is the opposite, friend. The verse says strong drink "…is bitter to those who consume it." (Isaiah 24:9) Bitter is the word that fits the blank.

I wish it were refreshing, friend. But Isaiah says the people no longer sing and drink wine, and that strong drink "…is bitter to those who consume it." (Isaiah 24:9) Bitter is the word that fits the blank.
Dancing isn't in this verse, friend. Isaiah says "All joy turns to gloom…" and that's the word that fits the blank. The tambourines have ceased and the harp is silent in the verse before it.
True, baker. Isaiah says, "The city is left in ruins; its gate is reduced to rubble." (Isaiah 24:12) The city is in ruins and its gate is rubble. Easy one, but a good one to hold onto.

That's right, baker. The prophet says, "I am wasting away! I am wasting away! Woe is me." (Isaiah 24:16) Singing is heard from the ends of the earth, and he answers with a woe. I think he says it twice because he means it.

Relief would be a nice scene, friend, but the text has him say something else. The prophet says, "I am wasting away! I am wasting away! Woe is me." (Isaiah 24:16) He says it twice, and none of it sounds like relief.

That's right, baker. Isaiah says, "Whoever flees the sound of panic will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught in the snare." (Isaiah 24:18) Fleeing the panic lands in the pit, and climbing out of the pit lands in the snare. The verse before it says terror, pit and snare await the "…dweller of the earth." (Isaiah 24:17)
